Brand Archetype Assessment

Every brand carries a personality. This is the one under OT, found not by the quiz alone but by the working session that followed it.

The map

Twelve personalities, in four families.

Archetypes are the twelve personalities people recognize without being told. They sit in four families, each driven by a different human need. Here is the whole map before we place OT on it.

The twelve archetypes, grouped into four families by core drive
Leave a legacy
Outlaw, Magician, Hero
The drive to change things and leave a mark.
Pursue connection
Lover, Jester, Everyman
The drive to belong and be close to others.
Provide structure
Ruler, Caregiver, Creator
The drive to bring order and to take care.
Explore spirituality
Innocent, Sage, Explorer
The drive to seek and to understand.
What changed

The quiz heard the voice. The session found the identity.

This is the important update. The first questionnaire captured how OT sounds, which is why the Outlaw scored loudest. The working session asked who OT is, and the picture sharpened considerably.

Heard first, the quiz
Outlaw, loudest
The rebel read scored highest, with Ruler, Magician, and Caregiver clustered close behind. It captured the marketing voice, the everything you have been told is out of date register.
Found in the room, the session
Ruler and Magician, at the core
Once the questions asked who OT is rather than how OT sounds, the Outlaw stepped back into its role as the voice, and Ruler and Magician rose as the core, with Caregiver as the texture underneath.
The architecture

One identity, one voice, one texture.

The most useful way to hold OT is in three layers. The core is who the brand is. The voice is how it gets attention. The texture is how the relationship feels over time.

Core identityRuler and Magician

Who OT is underneath everything. The precision and authority of the Ruler, joined to the transformation the Magician promises. Exact, credible, and built on making men measurably better.

VoiceOutlaw

How OT speaks to get attention. Sharp, a little rebellious, everything you have been told is out of date. This lives in the copy and the campaigns. It is the part the first quiz heard loudest, and it is the voice, not the identity.

TextureCaregiver

How the relationship feels over time. Present and supportive, the devoted partner who checks in and carries the worry. It grounds the edge and keeps the brand human.

The four in play

What each archetype means for OT.

RulerCore identity

The definitive standard. Precision, authority, and command of the science, the brand that sets the bar rather than chasing it.

In the room, the first impression was unanimous, the gold standard and the most authoritative care. Under fire, the instinct was to cite the data and let the authority speak.

MagicianCore identity

Transformation. The promise of more good years, of the sand moved back to the top of the glass, of becoming the man you are capable of becoming.

In the room, the intro line and the one word both landed on transformation, and the campaign instinct was aspirational, the before and after.

OutlawVoice

The register that earns attention. It challenges the old way and says the quiet part out loud. It belongs in the marketing, not in the mark.

In the room, it was named plainly as the marketing voice for eyeballs, with the note that the brand itself, and the logo, should not be challenging.

CaregiverTexture

The devoted partner. Structure and support, always in your corner, carrying the worry so the patient does not have to.

In the room, for the ongoing relationship, the devoted partner won over the commanding chief.

The one sentence version: OT talks like an Outlaw and organizes like a Ruler, with the Magician's transformation as the promise and the Caregiver's warmth in the service. That is the brief the guidelines and the mark both answer to.

What it means for the brand

Look impeccable. Talk boldly.

The identity sets the look, minimal, precise, and premium, the Ruler grounded by the Magician's transformation. The Outlaw stays in the copy and the campaigns, where a little edge earns attention, and it stays out of the mark. The next page turns that into color and type.

OT Brand Book · Page 02

Brand Guidelines

A minimal, premium system that reads the way the assessment does, the Ruler's precision and the Magician's transformation, never the Outlaw's edge.

The through line

Precision that transforms.

Two ideas run through everything, straight from the assessment. The first is the Ruler's precision, the definitive standard, exact and in command of the science. The second is the Magician's transformation, the promise of more good years. The Outlaw voice can stay sharp where it earns attention, but the brand itself should look calm, exact, and quietly premium. Talk boldly, look impeccable.

Color

Gold, led. Choose the temperature.

Gold is the through line, so each direction keeps a gold and then goes its own way. One is a high contrast luxury, the other a brighter lifestyle. Five colors each, all elevated, and each shown in both light and dark. These are the two we think fit OT best.

Type

An editorial serif, kept modern by a clean sans.

The serif brings authority and a little luxury, the Ruler. The sans keeps it current and easy to read. Three pairings to react to, each showing the OT monogram, a headline, and body.

Light and dark

One system, two modes.

Every palette ships with a light value and a dark value, so the brand holds either way. This whole book runs that switch. Try the control at the top right, the pages move from warm paper to near black, and the gold carries across both.

Next
Two choices unlock the rest.
First, which palette feels most like OT, the high contrast luxury or the bright lifestyle. Second, which type pairing carries it. Once we have those two, we build the full system out from them, the tints, the states, and the type scale.
OT Brand Book · Page 03

The Marks

Every mark should read the way the assessment does, the Ruler's restraint and the Magician's symbol, never the Outlaw's edge. Tap any mark to see it larger.

The full range

All nineteen marks.

The complete set, one through nineteen, each in three finishes. Sit with them. Most run black on white, gold on black, then white on black. Numbers 01 and 02 keep two tones, since the T inside them only reads when its color stays separate. Tap any mark to open it full size.

01O and T locked into one monogram. The T reads only in two tones.
02A T rising through a broken ring, on the same two-tone T.
03An angular interlock that reads as stacked initials.
04The hourglass at its purest. One clean shape, the whole idea.
05A drawn hourglass held between two plates. Technical, architectural.
06A bold, solid hourglass. Holds up at the smallest sizes.
07O and T fused into a serif ligature. The typographic route.
08A T whose stem becomes an hourglass, set in a ring.
09A double helix. The personalized, biological side of the story.
10A columned TO emblem. Formal and monumental.
11A single ribbon drawing an hourglass in one continuous line.
12Two facing arcs, the hourglass held in the space between.
13A geometric bowtie hourglass in clean outline.
14Two mirrored strokes with a waist between them. The softest mark.
15A filled hourglass with rounded corners. Warm and solid.
16Stacked bars narrowing to a center. An hourglass read as levels.
17A thin, angular hourglass outline. Precise and light.
18A pinched hourglass with concave sides. Taut and drawn in.
19The monogram sealed in a ring. The most badge-like of the set.
